title: One finite torsion level detects a split-torus normalizer over any ring
statement: Let $A$ be any commutative ring, $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], and let $G\to S$ be a smooth affine group scheme of finite presentation [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, pqf-def-affine-morphism, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. A group scheme is a group object in schemes over $S$ [def-pc-scheme], with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams. Finite presentation means locally of finite presentation, quasi-compact and quasi-separated [def-weil-pbc-scheme-conventions]. Let $r\geq0$ and let $T\hookrightarrow G$ be a closed subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] identified with $\mathbf G_{m,S}^{r}$, where $\mathbf G_m(W)=\Gamma(W,\mathcal O_W)^\times$ [def-sfb-relative-torus]. For $n\geq1$, define $T[n]=\ker([n]:T\to T)$; in these coordinates it is $\operatorname{Spec}A[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]/(t_1^n-1,\ldots,t_r^n-1)$, with its inherited group law. There exists an integer $n\geq1$ such that for every $S$-scheme $W$ and every $g\in G(W)=\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,G)$ one has $$gT_Wg^{-1}=T_W\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad gT[n]_Wg^{-1}=T[n]_W.$$ Here $K_W=K\times_SW$ [def-pc-fibre-product] and equality means equality of subgroup functors on every $W$-scheme. The single integer $n$ works for all $W$, so the equivalence persists under every base change of $S$. No invertibility requirement on $n$ and no Noetherian assumption on $A$ are imposed. The zero ring and $r=0$ are allowed.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.1 proof, printed p.68, first paragraph (torsion-level stabilization); Proposition 2.1.2 proof, printed pp.57-58, finite-presentation reduction to a finitely generated integer subalgebra and universal torsion density. The assertion is the split-torus, affine-base version of that reduction, with the stabilizing level retained after arbitrary base change. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this group-scheme structural assertion.

proof.text: Since $G\to S$ is affine and $S=\operatorname{Spec}A$, write $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$. Applying lem-weil-pbc-lfp-affine-opens-finite-presentation to the full affine opens gives a finite presentation of $B$ over $A$. Write $L=A[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$; by [lem-a1-locally-ringed-space-affine-adjunction] an $S$-morphism $V\to\operatorname{Spec}L$ is exactly an $r$-tuple in $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)^\times$, so $\operatorname{Spec}L$ represents $\mathbf G_{m,S}^r$ and $T\cong\operatorname{Spec}L$. Here $L$ is the ring of finite formal sums indexed by $\mathbf Z^r$, with $t^ut^v=t^{u+v}$. The closed immersion corresponds to a surjective $A$-algebra map $\pi:B\twoheadrightarrow L$; put $I=\ker\pi$.

source.place: Tag 01TQ, lemma-locally-finite-presentation-characterize, (1) implies (2); affine closed-immersion description in Tag 01QO.

proof.text: Choose a polynomial surjection $P=A[x_1,\ldots,x_d]\twoheadrightarrow B$ using the presentation of $B$. The algebra $L$ is finitely presented over $A$: use variables $t_i,u_i$ and relations $t_iu_i-1$, evaluating $u_i$ at $t_i^{-1}$. The inverse sends negative powers of $t_i$ to powers of $u_i$, so the two maps are inverse on finite monomial sums. Hence the composite surjection $P\twoheadrightarrow L$ has a finitely generated kernel by lem-weil-pbc-finite-presentation-surjection-kernel-fg. If its generators are $h_1,\ldots,h_m$, their images $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ in $B$ generate $I$: lift $b\in I$ to $p\in P$; then $p$ belongs to that kernel, and a generator expression for $p$ descends to one for $b$.

Let $c:G\times_ST\to G$ be the morphism $(g,t)\mapsto gtg^{-1}$, using the given inclusion of $T$. Its coordinate map is $c^*:B\to B[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$. Indeed, a map from this latter ring to an $A$-algebra $R$ is precisely a map $B\to R$ together with $r$ units of $R$, and by [lem-a1-locally-ringed-space-affine-adjunction] the same holds with $R$ replaced by $\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_V)$ for every scheme $V$, so $\operatorname{Spec}B[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]$ has the fibre-product universal property of $G\times_ST$. For any $\gamma:B\to R$, specialization of $c^*$ along $\gamma$ is the coordinate map of conjugation by the corresponding $g\in G(R)$ restricted to $T_R$; this follows by composition of the multiplication and inverse morphisms. Expand $c^*(f_j)=\sum_{u\in F_j}b_{ju}t^u$, with each $F_j\subset\mathbf Z^r$ finite. This uses only the definition of a Laurent polynomial.

source.place: Proposition 2.1.2 proof, printed pp.57-58: universal conjugation and torsion restrictions; agent coordinate expansion in the split case.

proof.text: Put $F=\bigcup_jF_j$ and choose $M\geq0$ bounding all $|u_i|$ for $u\in F$ and $1\leq i\leq r$; use $M=0$ when there are none. Choose $n=2M+2$. If $u,v\in F$ have the same image in $(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$, every $u_i-v_i$ is divisible by $n$ and has absolute value at most $2M<n$, hence is zero. Thus reduction modulo $n$ is injective on $F$. This choice depends only on the finitely many universal polynomials, before any choice of $R$ or $g$.

source.place: Example 2.1.9, printed p.62: finite Laurent-support version of the torsion-density calculation, with an explicit uniform bound supplied here.

proof.text: For every commutative ring $R$, apply lem-sfb-subgroup-algebra-coset-presentation with additive group $D=(\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^r$, subgroup $0$, no free factors, $r$ cyclic factors of order $n\geq2$, and their standard generators. It gives the isomorphism $R[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]/(t_i^n-1)_i\cong R[D]$ sending $t_i$ to $e_{\bar e_i}$. In the finitely supported group algebra, $e_a$ form an $R$-basis by def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group. Therefore the image of $\sum_ua_ut^u$ has coefficient $\sum_{u\bmod n=v}a_u$ at $e_v$. For support contained in $F$, injectivity in step 4 makes each such sum contain at most one coefficient. Consequently vanishing in this quotient forces every $a_u=0$. This holds also for $R=0$ and $r=0$, by the same basis statement.

source.place: Theorem 12.9(b), printed pp.233-234; arbitrary-ring coset presentation in the cited node, applied to a finite product of cyclic groups. Agent finite-support consequence.

proof.text: Let $R$ be any $A$-algebra and $g\in G(R)$, with coordinate map $\gamma:B\to R$. Suppose $gT[n]_Rg^{-1}=T[n]_R$. In particular $c_g:T[n]_R\to G_R$ factors through $T_R$. On coordinate rings this says the image of each $f_j$ is zero in $R[t_i^{\pm1}]/(t_i^n-1)_i$: a homomorphism factors through $B/I$ exactly when it kills $I$. These images are the classes of $\sum_{u\in F_j}\gamma(b_{ju})t^u$. Step 5 forces all $\gamma(b_{ju})=0$, so $c_g:T_R\to G_R$ itself kills $I$ and factors through $T_R$. The hypothesis also holds for $g^{-1}$. Apply the same argument, with the same $n$, to $g^{-1}$; thus both conjugations carry $T_R$ into itself. Composing them, which gives the identity, proves $gT_Rg^{-1}=T_R$ as subgroup functors on all $R$-schemes.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.1 proof, printed p.68, first paragraph; agent uniform split-coordinate proof replacing the Noetherian reduction by steps 2-5.

proof.text: Conversely, if conjugation by $g$ preserves $T_R$, it induces an automorphism of the group functor $T_R$. For any $R$-scheme $V$ and $t\in T_R(V)$, $(gtg^{-1})^n=gt^ng^{-1}$ by cancellation of adjacent $g^{-1}g$. Thus $t^n=1$ implies $(gtg^{-1})^n=1$, and the same implication for $g^{-1}$ gives equality of the kernels of $[n]$. This proves $gT[n]_Rg^{-1}=T[n]_R$, on every $V$ and not just on $R$-valued points.

source.place: Theorem 2.3.1 proof, printed p.68: preservation of torsion under a group-scheme automorphism; group calculation written out.

proof.text: For a general $S$-scheme $W$, restrict $g\in G(W)$ to any affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq W$ and apply steps 6-7. These restrictions use the original integer $n$. The local factorizations of $c_g:T_W\to G_W$ through $T_W$ agree on overlaps: after composition with the subgroup inclusion they equal $c_g$, and a subgroup functor inclusion is injective on every test scheme. The schemes $T_U$ form an open cover of $T_W$, so lem-weil-pbc-scheme-morphism-gluing glues the factors uniquely. Apply this also to $g^{-1}$, and use uniqueness in that lemma to check their composites are identity maps. Thus the subgroup-functor equality holds over $W$. The converse follows directly from the kernel calculation in step 7 on every $W$-scheme. Under a further base change the same morphisms and inverse identities pull back by the fibre-product universal property, so the same $n$ works. For $A=0$ all test schemes are empty. For $r=0$ the torus is the identity subgroup. Both cases are included; one may also take $n=1$ in either. No reducedness or invertibility was used.

source.place: Tag 01JJ, lemma-glue-functors, proof (gluing morphisms); application to the torsion-level argument of Conrad Theorem 2.3.1, printed p.68.
